title: The Real Learning Value of Kids Playing Many Kinds of Games
author: Shari Keller
source: Quest for Learning (Shari Keller Substack), January 12, 2026
summary: Keller pushes back on the adult question 'but what are they learning?' when children play games, arguing that games don't primarily teach content — they train the systems that make learning possible. The pathway she traces is Executive Function → Fluency → Mastery, and it depends on rotating through many kinds of games (strategy, physical, cooperative, imaginative) rather than on one good game played deeply. Rotating games is cognitive interleaving: each new game forces the brain to learn a new rule set, adjust to different social dynamics, transfer prior strategies imperfectly, and abandon what no longer fits, which produces the productive friction that drives learning. Games with high social interaction matter most because other people introduce unpredictability that defeats scripts. Executive function learned through play sticks because kids own the skills (using them because they work in a context that matters) rather than complying with a strategy. The piece names the common adult error: optimising 'educational' games for predetermined outcomes kills the iteration, exploration, failure, and surprise that make games powerful. The reframe: the question isn't whether a game is educational, it's what executive demands the game offers and how much room it leaves for unique solutions.
points: Games train executive function (planning, focus, working memory, flexible thinking, resilience) under real conditions, which is why kids own the skills they learn through play rather than complying with a strategy.

Rotating game types (strategy, physical, cooperative, imaginative) produces cognitive interleaving — friction that drives faster learning by forcing the brain to abandon prior scripts and adjust to new rule sets.
Social games matter most because other people introduce unpredictability; you can't run the same script twice and have to read the room, adjust, and recover.
Weak EF in kids isn't a character flaw or an explanation deficit; it's a real-life-practice deficit, and games naturally exercise planning, resilience, working memory, and flexibility every turn.

Adults kill the value of 'educational' games when they optimise for predetermined outcomes; real games work because they allow exploration, iteration, failure, and surprise — kill those and intrinsic motivation crashes.
quotes: When adults talk about kids and games, the conversation usually collapses into a single question: 'But what are they learning?' It sounds reasonable. But it misses where the real learning is happening. Because games don't primarily teach content. They train the systems that make learning possible in the first place.

When kids rotate games, strategy games, physical games, cooperative games, imaginative games, or play games that have a lot of moving parts, they're doing something cognitively powerful without knowing the term for it. They're interleaving.
All the different rules, social dynamics, strategies and challenges/fails/iterations create friction, meaning more mental effort. That friction matters because it is what helps kids learn faster.

You can explain executive function skills to kids: planning, focus, working memory, flexible thinking, resilience. But explanation doesn't equal ownership. Kids who learn EF through play learn it by doing, which means they own those skills.
Kids don't have weak executive function because they lack explanations. They have weak EF because they don't get enough real-life practice.

When a game starts feeling like school — when the outcome is predetermined and there's no room to iterate and discover a unique experience or solution — kids' intrinsic motivation crashes. Kids zone out.

The question isn't: 'Is this game educational?' It's: 'What exploration (read executive demands) does this game offer my child, and how much room does it leave for unique solutions?'” Archived from Quest for Learning (Shari Keller Substack) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
